entries.title: Bears' Rome Odunze among stars in Adidas' 'Speed Broker' ad campaign
entries.summary: <p>Expect to see even more of <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears" target="_blank" >Bears </a>receiver <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears/2026/06/01/bears-wr-rome-odunze-does-spot-on-bob-ross-impression-in-teams-schedule-release-video" target="_blank" >Rome Odunze</a> on your television screen this year.</p><p>The Bears receiver is part of Adidas’ national campaign, entitled “Speed is Money” and starring Chad “Ochocinco” Johnson. Johnson plays a “speed broker” who keeps track of nine fast football players, including six who play in the NFL —Jaguars receiver/cornerback Travis Hunter, Buccaneers receiver Emeka Egbuka, Lions receiver Amon-Ra St. Brown, Jets receiver Garrett Wilson, Falcons tight end Kyle Pitts and Odunze. The ad features a member of the USA women’s flag football team and two high school players.</p><p>Adidas signed Odunze to its athlete roster the night of the 2024 draft, when the Washington receiver was picked ninth overall by the Bears. He and Michael Penix Jr., another Adidas athlete, played together at Washington, which was also sponsored by the shoe company.</p><p>Odunze struggled with a foot injury last season, finishing with 44 catches for 661 yards in 12 games.</p>
entries.author: Patrick Finley

entries.title: Cubs sticking with Dansby Swanson in everyday lineup with hopes of jumpstarting shortstop’s slumping bat
entries.summary: <p>The <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs" >Cubs</a> don’t seem to have any plans to bench Dansby Swanson.</p><p>A prime target of frustrated fans during the team’s ongoing offensive struggles, Swanson is in <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs/2026/06/01/cubs-dansby-swanson-slump-stats-defense-craig-counsell-lineup" >the most recognizably bad spot statistically</a> of any Cubs regular, coming into Wednesday’s game with a .175 batting average that ranked as the worst in the sport among qualified hitters.</p><p>But Cubs brass, asked if it’s time to make a change at shortstop, did not indicate there’s a plot to move Swanson – the second highest paid player on the roster, with a $28 million salary – from his everyday role.</p><p>“Obviously, Dansby has struggled,” team president Jed Hoyer said Tuesday. “He’s gotten some days off. He’s working hard to improve. The offense has been a challenge, overall. It shouldn’t be, in general. We should score plenty of runs, but that hasn’t been the case.</p><p>“Our run prevention is probably the backbone of this team. … We prevent runs really well. We won a game in San Francisco the other day <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs/2026/06/13/cubs-michael-busch-defense-first-base-nico-hoerner-gold-glove-craig-counsell" >because we played great defense</a>, honestly. So you can’t just forget about that when we start to struggle a bit offensively.</p><p>“We can’t just run away from our run prevention at times when we struggle offensively.”</p><p>Indeed, Swanson continues to play excellent defense while scuffling at the plate, something that can be said about the team as a whole. A year after the Cubs won the team Gold Glove, they’re again the best defensive team in baseball, according to multiple metrics. That is valuable enough to the Cubs that they’d rather not pluck Swanson from the lineup.</p><p>But that doesn’t mean they’re satisfied with Swanson as a sub-.200 hitter, and they’re hoping his continued presence in the lineup will eventually jumpstart his frigid bat.</p><p>“I think we should be continuing to invest in Dansby getting back to the offensive player that we know he is,” manager Craig Counsell said Wednesday. “That’s what needs to happen for this team. That’s important to keep trying to do, and the best way to do that is to have him out on the field.”</p><p>Swanson has never exactly been an offensive menace, statistically. He’s a slightly below league-average hitter in his career, with an OPS-plus of 96. Coming into Wednesday, he was a .235 hitter with a .705 OPS in four seasons in a Cubs uniform.</p><p>But in addition to flashing a fantastic glove, he has swung a bat far more capable than it has been so far this season. Just last year, he hit 24 homers, the third highest single-season total in his career. He’s currently walking at a higher clip than at any point in his career, with a 12.7 percent walk rate.</p><p>Some might see increased playing time for reserve infielder – and the organization’s No. 2 prospect – Pedro Ramirez as an enticing alternative to the slumping Swanson. Ramirez has nine hits in his first 35 career at-bats, including his first career homer last weekend in San Francisco and a couple hits after entering the game as a pinch hitter in Monday night’s walk-off win at Wrigley Field.</p><p>But while removing Swanson from the batting order on a somewhat permanent basis doesn’t appear to be happening, Counsell has pulled various levers to try to add some juice to Swanson’s spot in the lineup.</p><p>He’s given his shortstop multiple days off, as Hoyer alluded to, and he’s pinch hit for him late in games numerous times in recent weeks, including in consecutive games this week against the Rockies, with Counsell subbing in Michael Conforto on Monday and Ramirez on Tuesday.</p><p>Being removed for a pinch hitter could understandably be a shot to the confidence or simply rub a veteran player the wrong way. But Counsell’s been impressed with how Swanson has handled being subbed out.</p><p>“I think Dansby takes a lot of pride in that,” Counsell said. “It’s no fun getting pinch hit for in his situation. He’s on the top step cheering.</p><p>“I take note of that. I think that’s impressive. It’s easy to kick a player when he’s down, for his struggles. But that’s not easy to do for the player right there.”</p>
entries.author: Vinnie Duber

entries.title: Storm-weary Northwest Indiana cleans up as rain continues
entries.summary: <p>Nearly a week after a tornado tore through parts of Merrillville, Indiana, Earline Walker is still dealing with the fallout as more storms were predicted for later Wednesday.</p><p>“Our roof had big, large holes due to trees or limbs flying onto the property,” the 63-year-old Walker said Wednesday morning of the storm that hit last Thursday evening in this community about an hour south of Downtown Chicago.</p><p>While power was restored for much of the town by Monday evening, Walker’s home still doesn’t have any.</p><p>But that’s the least of her concerns. She’s more worried about strong storms and possible tornadoes predicted by the National Weather Service for Wednesday evening.</p><p>“I’m praying. I believe in God and that it’s all going to work out. I am hoping that it bypasses us,” Walker said at a Salvation Army food distribution site in Merrillville.</p><p>The weather service confirmed that the EF-2 tornado that hit parts of the town last Thursday was one of 20 to strike parts of the Chicago area and other towns in Northwest Indiana, from Bartlett, Illinois, to near Valparaiso, Indiana.</p><p>Hundreds of trees in Merrillville were either uprooted or had limbs broken off on the town’s northern end near Gary, cutting an east-west path that saw two schools and dozens of businesses sustaining damage. As many as 200 buildings, including homes, sustained damage, according to Merrillville officials.</p><p>The storm knocked out power to more than 86,000 customers of Northern Indiana Public Service Co. As of Wednesday, NIPSCO reported power had been restored to most of its customers. But about 1,000 customers were still without power.</p><p>Walker’s husband and son helped to patch her home’s roof with leftover shingles from an earlier roof replacement project.</p><p>Walker said she never thought a storm of that strength would ever hit her home.</p><p>“We survived it. I’m grateful to God. If it had not been for God, I don’t believe we would have survived the way we did,” said Walker, who has lived in Merrillville for 13 years. “I am sorry for other people, the residents that lost their homes entirely. They might be homeless now and I’m very sad about that.”</p><p>For nearly a week, members of the Salvation Army of Northwest Indiana have been distributing food, cleaning supplies and clothing to nearly 400 affected residents of Merrillville.</p><p>“We’re helping the volunteers as well as helping to clean up the area,” said Jim Prichard, auxiliary captain for the Gary office of the Salvation Army. “We're out here serving lunches, water, snacks, whatever they may need, and pointing them in the right direction wherever we can to assist the residents.”</p><p>Prichard said the people who access services seem to have been staggered by the storm.</p><p>“They are very overwhelmed. They’re lost and they just need reassurance that there are people out there to help,” Prichard said.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure Despite her own home’s basement being flooded in southern Porter County, Murkve said she wanted to be in Merrillville to help out.</p><p>“This has been the most devastating that I have seen in Northwest Indiana,” Murkve said. “I'd rather help somebody else. I can take care of my concerns when I get home, but I'm here to serve the people right now that need the most help and doing the most good here.”</p><p>Another group of volunteers with the Los Angeles-based Team Rubicon have been assisting those impacted with disaster cleanup at no cost to homeowners. The Lake County, Indiana, Emergency Management Agency invited Team Rubicon to assist homeowners.</p><p>“We're running chainsaws and mucking out houses. We've already been in contact with about 25 to 30 homeowners that we're either already starting to help or will be helping shortly,” said Maureen Kerrigan of Team Rubicon. “Every homeowner after a big disaster does feel lost. One of our high points is that we give them hope. We give them a place to start.”</p><p>Even as cleanup continues, many businesses and government offices closed early on Wednesday due to the oncoming storm.</p><p><i>Michael Puente is a reporter and weekend anchor with WBEZ.</i><br></p>

entries.title: Thomas R. Donovan, patronage chief under Richard J. Daley and former CBOT president, dies at 88
entries.summary: <p></p><p></p><p></p><p>In the 1970s, Thomas R. Donovan proudly served as Mayor Richard J. Daley's patronage chief — doling out jobs that were the lifeblood of the city's Democratic machine.</p><p>It was an era that gave Chicago politics the well-worn expression, “We don’t want nobody nobody sent.”</p><p>Patronage wasn't a dirty word yet. It was just how things worked.</p><p>The federal court-ordered Shakman decrees, which made the long-held practice illegal, were still a few years away.</p><p>"Daley made the final decisions on whether a particular ward got X number of jobs, and which ones, but Donovan lined up the requests and sent out the orders," said Dick Simpson, professor emeritus at the University of Illinois Chicago and a former alderman who led a machine opposition bloc after his election in 1971.</p><p>When Mayor Richard J. Daley died in office on Dec. 20, 1976, Mr. Donovan was chief among the Democratic heavyweights who anointed Michael Bilandic his successor.</p><p>A mostly pliant City Council voted Bilandic in as acting mayor until a special election could be held six months later, which Bilandic won.</p><p>Bilandic was a status quo leader who ensured the way things were under Daley would remain.</p><p>"Donovan linked up elements of the business community and the elements of the Democratic Party who were loyal to the Bridgeport-centered Daley machine, who basically agreed that Bilandic wasn't going to rock the boat too much," Simpson said.</p><p>Mr. Donovan remained as patronage czar and adviser in the Bilandic administration.</p><p>Bilandic occupied the mayor's office on the fifth floor of City Hall and received all the accompanying attention of ribbon cuttings and presiding over City Council meetings, but Mr. Donovan, it was said, was the backroom political broker to whom people in the know turned to for favors.</p><p>A 1977 Chicago Daily News story headlined "Meet the man who controls the patronage" opened with the lines: "One of the most influential men in City Hall these days is a quiet unassuming former construction worker from Bridgeport named Thomas R. Donovan. He is not well known to the majority of Chicagoans, but anyone who wants a favor from the mayor's office knows Donovan is the one to turn to."</p><p>Mr. Donovan left the mayor's office after Bilandic lost the 1979 mayoral contest to Jane Byrne — a defeat many attributed to discontent over Bilandic's failure to clear the roads when a blizzard buried Chicago in snow just days before the election.</p><p>Mr. Donovan took a job as secretary at the Chicago Board of Trade. In 1983, he became CBOT's long-serving president and chief executive officer.</p><p>Mr. Donovan died Sunday. His family did not share a cause of death. He was 88.</p><p>Mr. Donovan was born Sept. 13, 1937, and was raised in Bridgeport.</p><p>He graduated from De La Salle Institute and took classes at the University of Illinois' Navy Pier campus while working toward joining the glaziers union, whose workers install storefront framing and glass. He worked at Hamilton Glass Co. from 1956 to 1964, after which he took a job in the Chicago Park District's maintenance department.</p><p>In 1969, he got a job in the accounting office of the Department of Streets and Sanitation. The commissioner at the time, James McDonough, impressed by Mr. Donovan, mentioned him to Mayor Daley, which quickly paved the way for a job in City Hall.</p><p>Mr. Donovan soon found himself the beneficiary of a reshuffle of personnel in the mayor's office that led him to become patronage chief.</p><p>Attending night classes, Mr. Donovan earned his bachelor's degree in business and economics from the Illinois Institute of Technology in 1972 and a master's degree in public administration from the school in 1975.</p><p>Mr. Donovan was also the founding chairman of Quantum Crossings, a company that provides security, technology and electrical services.</p><p>Mr. Donovan is survived by his wife, Vita Donovan, and children. </p><p>A visitation will be held from 3-9 p.m. Friday at Robert J. Sheehy & Sons Funeral Home in Orland Park.</p><p>A funeral Mass will be held at 11:30 a.m. Saturday at St. Alexander Parish in Palos Heights.</p>

entries.title: Meet the mega-donors who funded the Obama Foundation
entries.summary: <p>For the first time we have more information about how much the very top donors to the Obama Presidential Foundation contributed. We know more now because there is a donor wall in the museum giving the mega-givers a nod. Through the years I’ve been covering Obama Foundation finances, this is the most comprehensive breakdown to date.</p><p>The foundation collected six donations of $50 million plus, including one anonymous contributor.</p><p>The names listed on the wall are:</p><p><b>Connie Ballmer.</b> An Obama Foundation board member, Ballmer is a general partner and founding investor at Blue Meridian Partners and serves on the boards of StriveTogether and the Los Angeles Clippers Foundation. The Eleanor Roosevelt Fruit & Vegetable Garden is supported by Ballmer and her husband, Steven Ballmer, the former Microsoft CEO.</p><p><b>Jeff Bezos</b>. The founder of Amazon, owner of the Washington Post and of Blue Origin, the spaceflight company, among other enterprises, donated $100 million. As part of the gift, Bezos asked that the Plaza at the Obama Presidential Center be named for the late Rep. John Lewis, D-Ga., the civil rights icon who died in 2020.</p><p><b>Brian Chesky</b>. The Airbnb CEO and co-founder donated $125 million. As far as is known to the public, that's the biggest contribution to the foundation.</p><p>The Chesky gift earmarks $100 million for the Obama-Chesky Voyager scholarship for public service. Per the Obama web site: “The Voyager Scholarship Program is a two-year leadership development and scholarship program. Through a transformational combination of barrier-reducing financial aid, an immersive work-travel experience, and a robust network of leaders and mentors, the Voyager Scholarship is designed to inspire, empower, and connect the next generation of leaders and equip them with the tools and resources they need to launch their careers in public service.”</p><p>As I <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/columnists/2023/8/8/23825036/obama-foundation-fueled-by-two-mega-donors-has-record-fundraising-year-in-2022" >wrote</a> in 2023, “The first class of Voyager Public Service Scholarship recipients launched in 2022. Voyager scholarships provide up to $50,000 to students starting their junior year in college plus a $10,000 stipend and free Airbnb housing for a summer work-travel project. The remaining $25 million of the Chesky contribution is unrestricted and can be used for Obama Center construction.”</p><p><b>Hutchins Family Foundation</b>. Glenn Hutchins is the Vice chair of the Obama Foundation. Glenn Hutchins is the co-founder of Silver Lake investments, the chairman of North Island and North Island Ventures and from 2003-2025 was part of the Boston Celtics ownership group.</p><p>The Hope and Change Lobby at the center was made possible through the Hutchins Family Foundation donation.</p><p>There are 12 contributions between $25 million and $49.9 million, including one anonymous giver.</p><p><b>Michelle Yee & Reid Hoffman – Aphorism Foundation</b>. Hoffman is the CEO of LinkedIn and a major Obama political donor who was an early contributor to the foundation.</p><p><b>Patti Bao & Tony Xu</b>. Xu is a co-founder of DoorDash.</p><p><b>Lynne & Marc R. Benioff</b>. Marc Benioff is Chair, Chief Executive Officer and Co-Founder of Salesforce. Lynne Benioff is the Time Magazine cochair. Obama appointed Lynne Benioff to the Presidio Trust board in 2015. She rejoined the Presido Board last month, tapped by President Donald Trump.</p><p><b>The Bob Clark Family</b>. Clark is the founder of the Chicago based Clayco construction firm. He has been close to Obama and is a major Democratic donor. Clark has been involved in the development of the center in Jackson Park since the beginning. Clayco helped manage the project.</p><p><b>The Crimson Lion/Lavine Family Foundation</b>. Jonathan Lavine served as Co-Managing Partner of Bain Capital, LP from 2016 – 2024 and chair until this year, when he became a senior advisory partner. Lavin and wife Jeannie founded the Crimson Lion Foundation. Obama appointed Lavine to the United States Holocaust Memorial Council board in December 2016.</p><p>Their foundation’s donation funded the Rabbi Abraham Joshua Heschel Exhibition Gallery, The People's House on the fourth level of the museum.</p><p><b>Gates Foundation</b>. The Gates Foundation was created by Microsoft co-founder Bill Gates.</p><p><b>Hobson/Lucas Family Foundation</b>. Mellody Hobson is the Co-CEO Chairman of the Board of Trustees, Ariel Investment Trust, based in Chicago with deep connections to the city. Ariel was founded by John Rogers, whose connections to Barack and Michelle Obama and Valerie Jarrett, the foundation CEO, goes back decades. George Lucas is the Hollywood producer, writer and director.</p><p>The gift funded the John W. Rogers, Jr. Exhibition Gallery, Working for the Common Good, in the Obama Presidential Center Museum.</p><p><b>Sean & Alexandra Parker</b>. Sean Parker is a member of the Obama Foundation Board. He founded Facebook with Mark Zuckerberg in 2004 and served as its first president.</p><p><b>Pritzker Traubert Family</b>. The 2008 presidential campaign of then-Sen. Obama became viable because of the money raised by Chicago’s Penny Pritzker, his national finance chair. Pritzker is a business executive, civic leader and philanthropist who served as Obama’s Commerce Secretary in his second term. She co-founded the Pritzker Traubert Foundation with her husband, Dr. Bryan Traubert. She is on the Obama Foundation board. The Elie Wiesel Auditorium in the forum was funded by the Pritzker Traubert Family.</p><p><b>Stavros Niarchos Foundation (SNF)</b>. Stavros Niarchos is a Greek shipping magnate. While president, Obama, on Nov. 16, 2016, delivered a speech at the Niarchos foundation in Athens during his first trip to Greece. The gift went towards the Democracy in Action Lab in the lower level of the Forum building.</p><p><b>The Family of Jessie Reid Taylor</b>. The gift from the family gift supported the Paul Farmer Special Exhibitions Gallery in the lower level of the museum.</p><p>***</p><p>Selected Chicago-connected names you may recognize who gave between $10 million and $24.9 million.</p><p>Alphawood Foundation, Fred Eychaner, chair; The Boeing Company; the Crown family; John D. and Catherine T. MacArthur Foundation; Michael Jordan & Family; Fay & Daniel Levin; Joe & Rika Mansueto; Northwestern Medicine; Cari & Michael Sacks; The University of Chicago and Oprah Winfrey.</p>

entries.title: You want stories? Cubs legend Billy Williams, who just turned 88, has some stories
entries.summary: <p>COOPERSTOWN, N.Y. — Billy Williams played his last game for the Cubs in 1976. It was the 100th year of the Cubs, the bicentennial of our nation, the summer that his teammate, center fielder and U.S. Marine Reservist Rick Monday, snatched an American flag away from two intruders, father and son, about to set it on fire on the Dodger Stadium grass.</p><p>Now it is 2026. The Cubs are celebrating their 150th season. The country is turning 250. The flag that Rick Monday saved is currently on display for the first time in all its frayed and faded glory in the baseball Hall of Fame here in this upstate New York village.</p><p>And Billy Williams, 49 years after being inducted into baseball’s Hall of Fame, is marking his 88th birthday.</p><p>“I look at 88 and I say, ‘You’re gettin’ old, boy,' ’’ he said by phone from his home in Glen Ellyn, “But then I think about, you know, God has protected me to get this far. And you know, I’ve seen grandkids. And now I’ve got three great-grandkids, So I look at that and say, He has spared me, to see my family grow.</p><p>“There’s still some time I got to be on earth. You think about it. You think about it because you think about how long you’ve lived and what you’ve learned through the years and what you could teach your kids and grandkids. What it’s all about, you know.</p><p>'‘You don’t get out of this world alive, nobody. You think about it. That’s why, matter of fact, I went to church this morning, and I tried to give praise and thanks. Because I was taught that by my grandfather, and taught that by mother, She inspired me, and I’m inspiring them to do these kinds of things. So 88, 88 is a nice age.''</p><p>Surely, you knew there would be stories. Too many to contain in a single column by your Sun-Times scribbler. Allow us to share a few more.</p><p><b>Nailed it: A bat that went 8-for-8</b> </p><p>Jon Shestakofsky, the Hall of Fame’s vice president of communications and content, has taken his visitor downstairs into the vault, which contains precious baseball artifacts that are not currently on exhibit. Donning plastic gloves, he hands your correspondent, who also puts on gloves, the bat that Billy Williams used when he went 8-for-8 in a double-header against Houston: 4-for-4 in the first game, 4-for-4 in the second.</p><p>“If you look down here,’’ Shestakosky said, pointing to the handle just below the Louisville Slugger label, “you can see there are nails.’’</p><p>Nails?</p><p>''Oh, that happens when you get a bat that fits you,’’ Williams says. “I had small hands. The handle was pretty good. It was comfortable to me. And I think it was a little cracked and stuff because somebody might have used it, some right-handed hitter might have used it. The grains had come up a little bit, and I think Yosh [Kawano, the legendary Cubs clubhouse man] might have stuck a couple of little nails in there.''</p><p>’’The rule book does not make allowances for hammering nails into a bat.</p><p>I probably went up there swinging it where the umpire couldn’t get a good eye on it,’’ he said, chuckling. “That was a good bat.''</p><p><b>Murcer learns about Wrigley's winds</b></p><p>Billy Williams is the only left-handed hitter in Cubs history to hit 40 or more home runs in a season, hitting 42 in 1970. Only Kyle Schwarber, with 38 in 2019, has come close.</p><p>Bobby Murcer, a left-handed-hitting center fielder who played for the Cubs in the ‘70s and once hit 33 home runs for the Yankees, hit 27 in 1977, his first season with the Cubs, then hit just nine the following year.</p><p>Like many folks who don’t live in Chicago, Murcer thought the wind always blew out at Wrigley Field.</p><p>“I say to him, ‘Well, when Ernie [Banks] and I retired, the wind changed and started blowing in,’ ’’ Williams said, laughing.</p><p><b>Billy vs. Bob Gibson</b></p><p>It ranks among the greatest Opening Days in franchise history, Two Hall of Famers on the mound, Bob Gibson for the Cardinals, Fergie Jenkins for the Cubs. Seven future Hall of Famers combined in the two lineups, Billy Williams among them.</p><p>April 6, 1971. The wind was blowing in. The temperature hovered around 40. The game was tied 1-1 and went into extra innings. Fergie was still pitching for the Cubs, Gibson for the Cardinals. It may have been the season opener, but both were pitching brilliantly.</p><p>Williams won it with a walk-off home run off Gibson in the bottom of the 10th. “Sometimes this game will drive a man crazy,’’ Gibson said afterward.</p><p>Williams, whose 10 career home runs off Gibson are the most by any player, would see Gibson frequently when Hall of Famers gathered for the annual induction ceremony. Did Williams ever remind Gibson of his home run?</p><p>“I’m laughing because we never talked about that,’’ Williams said. “He never mentioned that. You know he would never mention that. But while he was living, I didn’t mention it too much, either. He might have got a ball up there and knocked me down.’’</p><p><b>Bleacher creatures</b></p><p>Sorry, St. Louis. Long before a bunch of college kids from Texas showed up in your bleachers, took their shirts off, whipped them overhead and started the “Tarps Off” fad that’s showing up in ballparks all over the country, Wrigley Field had its Bleacher Bums.</p><p>Billy Williams was there for the birth of the Bums in 1969, when the Cubs, who spent most of the ‘60s playing in front of crowds the size of a family picnic, made a run for the pennant in ’69 and inspired a new generation of fans who turned the Wrigley bleachers into their personal playground, parading on top of the outfield wall, serenading their heroes, taunting the opposition, and occasionally toppling onto the field.</p><p>Those yellow baskets attached to the fence that catch home runs? That was not what they were designed for. They were there to keep overserved fans from taking headers onto the grass below.</p><p>“A lot of people up there were school teachers, who had the summer off. I remember one guy used to play the trumpet, couldn’t hit a single note, he just played.</p><p>“I used to have fun with them because they knew I drove a Wildcat Buick and every time I went out there they called me ‘Wildcat Willie.’ It was a fun time out there because they had a great time.’’</p><p>A better time than the Cubs, who blew a big lead in August and finished far behind the Miracle Mets.</p><p><b>And Billy's favorite memory of all</b></p><p>The fondest memory of all? It was the time they held Billy Williams Day and he brought his mother, Jesse May Williams, the woman who raised her family and took young Billy to the homes of the white folks whose washing and ironing and housekeeping she would do.</p><p>“She got a chance to be on the field with me,’’ he said, “and she enjoyed that moment. She said, ‘I’m going to be on that field with 40,000 people and I’m a gonna fall out.’ I said, ‘You’re not going to fall out, you’re not going to faint.' She brought her sister with her. </p><p>“I look at those pictures from time to time. That was a special moment for me.’’</p>

entries.title: New bodycam footage shows the deadly shooting of Chicago police officer Ella French
entries.summary: <p>Nearly five years after Chicago police officer Ella French was killed, oversight officials on Wednesday released video footage of the on-duty shooting — closing the book on a dark chapter in the city’s history. </p><p>Body camera footage shows the brief moments before a routine traffic stop <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/news/2021/8/8/22615487/chicago-police-officer-killed-ella-french-wounded-suspects-arrested-west-englewood-david-brown" target="_blank" >turned deadly</a> on Aug. 7, 2021. French was shot and killed and her partner, officer Carlos Yanez Jr., was seriously wounded.</p><p>Gunman Emonte Morgan and his brother, Eric, were arrested shortly after the attack. Court orders prohibited the release of any materials related to the shooting while their criminal cases played out.</p><p>Eric Morgan pleaded guilty to gun charges in 2023 and was sentenced to seven years in prison. It <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2024/03/05/chicago-police-officer-ella-french-jury-trial-emonte-morgan " target="_blank" >took a jury just hours</a> to find his older brother guilty of murder and attempted murder a year later. Emonte Morgan was sentenced to life in prison.</p><p>With those court orders no longer in effect, the Civilian Office of Police Accountability published the video footage online Wednesday afternoon.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center><div class="Enhancement-item"> <div class="ExternalContent-wrapper" data-embed> <iframe width="200" height="113" src="https://www.youtube.com/embed/S8XGtI8ZiFQ?feature=oembed" frameborder="0" allow="accelerometer; autoplay; clipboard-write; encrypted-media; gyroscope; picture-in-picture; web-share" referrerpolicy="strict-origin-when-cross-origin" allowfullscreen title="New body camera footage shows the deadly shooting of Chicago police officer Ella French"></iframe> </div> </div></div><p>“COPA is releasing this video in response to a request under the Freedom of Information Act (FOIA) and in keeping with our commitment to transparency and public accountability,” COPA Chief Administrator LaKenya White wrote in a statement.</p><p>“As we do so, it is important to remember that this video captures a profoundly tragic event. Our thoughts remain with Officer Ella French and Officer Carlos Yanez Jr., their loved ones, colleagues, and all those whose lives were forever changed by this incident.” </p><p>Jurors watched the jarring body camera footage during Emonte Morgan’s trial. </p><p>French and her two partners were on patrol in Englewood when they pulled over a Honda CR-V she believed had an expired registration. Emonte Morgan was in the back seat, where Yanez noticed an open alcohol container, video shows. French approached Eric Morgan in the driver's seat and told the SUV's occupants she could smell cannabis. </p><p>French patted down Eric Morgan near the front of the car, the footage shows. Meanwhile, her partners, Yanez and officer Joshua Blas, escorted Emonte Morgan and a young woman toward the back of the Honda.</p><p>The video shows Emonte Morgan argued with the officers as Yanez repeatedly told him to put away his phone and a drink he was holding. </p><p>“You’re doing too much, man,” Yanez said, as he and Blas led Emonte Morgan back toward the front of the car. </p><p>Then, Eric Morgan ran off and Blas chased after him. French went to the front of the SUV to help Yanez, who was pressed against Emonte Morgan, struggling to get control of his hand.</p><p>“Don’t move motherf-----” Yanez said. “Let me see your other hand.” </p><p>Seconds later, a scream is heard, along with the soft pop of a .22-caliber Glock handgun.</p><p>French’s body camera tilted upwards as she fell to the ground. Yanez’s camera also showed him falling backwards.</p><p>Blas’ camera captured him running back toward the shooting scene. Blas then opened fire, striking Emote Morgan in the arm and chest, prosecutors have said.</p><p>Emote Morgan ran to his brother and handed off the gun before collapsing from his injuries, prosecutors said. Eric Morgan fled to a nearby backyard, where he was held by a man hosting a barbecue until police arrived.</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/news/2021/8/8/22615487/chicago-police-officer-killed-ella-french-wounded-suspects-arrested-west-englewood-david-brown" target="_blank" >Slain Chicago police officer ‘wanted to do good for the world,’ brother says</a> </li> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https: //chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2024/03/05/chicago-police-officer-ella-french-jury-trial-emonte-morgan" target="_blank" >Jury takes just hours to convict man of killing Chicago Police Officer Ella French and wounding her partner</a> </li> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2024/09/11/sentencing-killing-chicago-police-officer-ella-french" target="_blank" >Mom of slain Chicago Police Officer Ella French confronts killer as he gets life in prison: ‘With our choices come consequences’</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p></p>

entries.title: Mayoral allies snuff out Ald. Beale's bid to ban sweepstakes machines to maximize take from video gambling
entries.summary: <p>Mayor Brandon Johnson scored a rare City Council victory on Wednesday when his allies snuffed out an attempt to ban sweepstakes machines that compete with and take revenue away from video gambling terminals.</p><p>Ald. Anthony Beale (9th) muscled the sweepstakes ban through <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/city-hall/2026/05/05/chicago-city-council-license-committee-sweepstakes-machine-ban" >the Council’s License Committee</a> over the mayor’s objections and hoped to convince the full Council to do the same — even as Johnson continues to lobby behind the scenes to<a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/city-hall/2026/06/11/mayor-brandon-johnson-repeal-video-gambling-bid-chicago" > repeal the ordinance</a> lifting the city's ban on video gambling terminals.</p><p>But Beale came up with the legislative equivalent of snake eyes. The vote was 33-15 to defeat the ban and allow roughly 7,000 sweepstakes machines to continue operating. </p><p>Sweepstakes gambling machines look like video slot machines but have managed to operate in a gray area of the law by offering “free play” options and coupons to winners instead of cash.</p><p>Budget Committee Chair Jason Ervin (28th) — Beale’s political nemesis and the mayor’s most powerful City Council ally — argued that sweepstakes machines are “not illegal machines. They’re amusement devices.”</p><p>He convinced his colleagues that African American businesses frozen out when the state legalized marijuana would be harmed the most because they own the majority of sweepstakes machines.</p><p>“Who signs up to put their own communities in peril? ... I took this job to do no harm. And this piece of legislation does harm,” Ervin said.</p><p>“Our folks are locked out of the VGT space, locked out of the cannabis space. In a legal sense, they have a method to participate and we want to take that away. Tell me what sense does that make? Did we sign up to come down here to take money out of the hands of Black folks? That makes no sense that we would sit back to take, literally by the stroke of a pen, money out of the community, out of the businesses in our respective communities.”</p><p>Beale was rankled by Ervin's remarks. </p><p>“What’s the difference between turning a blind eye [on sweepstakes machine operators and] the drug boy on the corner selling weed and selling cocaine? They’re employing youth, too. Are we going to turn a blind eye to them because I know them? 'I don’t want to hurt small businesses’? Come on, y’all,” Beale told his colleagues.</p><p>“This is a slam dunk for us to move forward to do what’s right to maximize the revenue from video gaming terminals that this body has approved, that we’re looking to get revenue from.”</p><p>Beale said there are “7,000 illegal sweepstakes machine that we know of” in Chicago, and that the cash-strapped city is not getting a dime from any of them because they are “not recognized” by the Illinois Gaming Board.</p><p>“There are some areas of the city that have 20 to 30 machines in a gas station. That’s a mini-casino operating illegally that we’re not getting a dime from,” Beale said.</p><p>The $16.6 billion, 2026 budget <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/city-hall/2025/12/23/mayor-brandon-johnson-city-council-alternate-budget" target="_blank" >approved by a City Council </a>majority lifted the Chicago ban on video gambling and assumed Chicago would generate $6.8 million by licensing newly legalized <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/city-hall/2025/09/16/video-gaming-in-chicago-proposal-anthony-beale-brandon-johnson" target="_blank" >video gambling terminals</a> across the city.</p><p>Johnson has raised strong objections to legalizing video gambling, in part because he believes it would violate the city’s host agreement with Bally’s, the gambling giant operating a temporary casino at Medinah Temple while building a permanent casino-entertainment complex in River West.</p><p>The mayor’s City Council allies have either banned or attempted to ban video gambling terminals in their individual wards while buying time for Johnson to find the votes to repeal the ordinance citywide. Wednesday’s action buys Johnson more time to round up those votes. </p><p></p><p>After the Council meeting, Johnson made the case for a “fair and open hearing to discuss all of the ramifications” of legalizing video gambling. </p><p>“There are some legitimate concerns — particularly around the amount of jobs that have been promised by the Bally’s casino,” he said. “I believe it’s imperative that this [Workforce Development] committee goes through a healthy debate so that we don’t … cause harm to the revenue that we are projecting to the casino, have a negative impact on the workforce, and that we make sure that we’re not in any way violating what the initial agreement called for.”</p><p>In a letter distributed to City Council members Wednesday, Bally's reiterated its argument that video gambling would cost the city $74 million in annual revenue and up to 1,050 jobs at its temporary and permanent casinos. It would force the city to renegotiate critical elements of its host agreement, wipe out a yearly $4 million lump sum payment from Bally’s, and shrink the casino jackpot needed to save police and fire pension funds.</p>

entries.title: Tiago Splitter brings foxhole mentality to his new Bulls coaching seat
entries.summary: <p>Tiago Splitter has been watching the Bulls from afar.</p><p>Not just Wednesday morning before his introductory press conference at the Advocate Center, not just earlier this season when he was a thousand miles away trying to right the ship in Portland, and not just years ago when he was a championship player in San Antonio.</p><p>“I’m actually a Bulls fan myself,” Splitter admitted. “Growing up in Brazil, I watched many games late at night, hidden from my parents at 1 am, watching MJ (Michael Jordan) games and rooting for the Bulls. So super excited to be here.”</p><p>A feeling that was very mutual.</p><p>Executive vice president of basketball operations Bryson Graham introduced Splitter as the organization’s 25<sup>th</sup> head coach and did so by first explaining how the month-long process ended with the former Trail Blazers interim coach. A process that began with a wide net, involved numerous zoom calls, whittled down to a final four of Minnesota assistant Micah Nori, Atanta’s Ryan Schmidt, and in-house candidate Wes Unseld Jr., and then led to the final decision.</p><p>“Couldn’t be more excited,” Graham said. “He’s what we’re looking for. Why Tiago? At the end of the day there are so many things we can go into but the things that stood out to me are he’s smart, he’s curious as a coach in a game that’s always changing, he wants to get better. He’s got the right level of competitiveness, he’s a good communicator, he connects well with players, he’s been in that locker room and won at a really high level, and he’s got a vision, and that is so important when you are embarking on something like this because we are at the ground floor.</p><p>“When you are going through a lot of hard times as a coach, whatever, a player, a front office staff, you’ve got to be in the foxhole with someone you trust, and there’s no one more that I want to be in that foxhole with than (Splitter).”</p><p>Especially with Splitter’s most recent “foxhole” experience.</p><p>The 41-year-old began his NBA coaching career in 2019, joining the Brooklyn Nets staff. But it was this last season that put him on the map, as he was vaulted from assistant to becoming the Trail Blazers’ head coach, inheriting a complete mess in the wake of former head man Chauncey Billups arrested in connection with an illegal gambling investigation.</p><p>In the wake of that news it felt like Portland was about to sink into the Association’s lottery basement, but Splitter had other ideas. Not only did he refocus the group to a 42-40 record and the play-in tournament but beat Phoenix in that first game to capture the No. 7 seed and make the postseason.</p><p>Along the way he helped Deni Avdija become a first-time All-Star and former No. 3 pick Scoot Henderson somewhat resurrected his young career, turning the Blazers into a grind-it-out, hard-hat group.</p><p>That didn’t go unnoticed and not just by Graham. Several teams were interested in Splitter, including the Trail Blazers.</p><p>Their ownership group blinked while Graham and the Bulls didn’t. As Splitter said several times during his presser, “now it’s time to get to work.”</p><p>“It’s going to be a lot of work, it’s going to take some time,” Splitter said. “I know what it takes and I know the responsibility I have and the expectations that come with being the head coach of the Chicago Bulls. I’m ready and I can’t wait to start and work.</p><p>“I have a vision, I have a way I want to play, but you also have to explore what they do best. That’s what we’re going to do here … I can guarantee you one thing: We’re going to compete every night and we’re going to have high standards with everything we do.”</p>
